query: How does goal achievement vary across department, metric, and the management practices described?

per_column.name: goal_outcome_domain
per_column.rationale: Cleanly derived from description/category and matches source in all samples. Somewhat redundant with the existing 'category' column (cost_reduction, customer_satisfaction, etc. mirror category values), which caps its analytical novelty, but it does offer a normalized grouping axis for the query's department/metric comparison.

per_column.name: implementation_lever_type
per_column.rationale: Directly addresses the 'management practices' axis of the query, giving a genuine new grouping dimension. Mostly well-grounded (resource_optimization, customer_interaction, training_engagement match text), but the revenue-growth row's 'resource_optimization' is a weak reading of 'increase premium subscriptions', showing some categorization slippage.

per_column.name: metric_alignment_clarity
per_column.rationale: Highly relevant to the query since 'metric' figures in the analysis; flagging whether the stated goal aligns with the assigned metric is analytically valuable. Samples show metrics like 'Expense Ratio' for customer satisfaction goals, correctly labeled misaligned. Near-constant skew (392 misaligned) reduces discriminating power somewhat but the signal is real and grounded.

per_column.name: stakeholder_engagement_signal
per_column.rationale: A bare boolean flag that adds modest leverage for the management-practices angle. All samples returned False despite the customer-satisfaction row mentioning 'personalized customer interactions' and 'after-sales support', suggesting the signal may under-fire, but no clear contradiction of source.

per_column.name: time_horizon_category
per_column.rationale: Useful new axis (immediate vs fiscal_year vs multi_year) for comparing achievement, and partially derivable from start/end dates too. Groundedness good: 'next fiscal year'->fiscal_year, 'compared to last quarter'->immediate_quarterly, 'upcoming year'->fiscal_year all match text.

per_column.name: outcome_specificity
per_column.rationale: Distinguishes end-state-defined vs direction-only vs milestone goals, a meaningful lens on goal quality tied to achievement. Samples largely sound: 'from 78% to 90%' -> end_state_defined; cost-reduction 20% row labeled improvement_direction_only is arguably understated but defensible.

per_column.name: improvement_mechanism
per_column.rationale: Adds a mechanism-of-change axis, but overlaps conceptually with implementation_lever_type, reducing independent value. Groundedness weaker: 'efficient communication channels' -> structural_reorganization and premium-subscription growth -> structural_reorganization are loosely warranted at best, indicating some imposed categorization not clearly in the text.

per_column.name: quantified_financial_impact
per_column.rationale: Boolean flag with limited but plausible value for the analysis. Groundedness is uneven: cost-reduction 20% row (True) is fine, but the customer-satisfaction row (78%->90% ratings, no dollar figure) marked True and the subscription row marked True stretch 'financial impact' beyond what the text quantifies, conflating any percentage with financial quantification.

judge.rationale: The added columns collectively open several genuine analytical axes aligned to the query's department/metric/management-practices framing: outcome domain, implementation lever, metric alignment, time horizon, and outcome specificity are meaningful grouping dimensions. Some columns are partly redundant (goal_outcome_domain vs existing category; improvement_mechanism vs implementation_lever_type) or bare booleans, tempering usefulness. Groundedness is generally sound for extractive/categorical columns, but a few inferential columns (improvement_mechanism, quantified_financial_impact) apply confident labels the source text does not clearly support, and quantified_financial_impact conflates any percentage target with financial quantification, producing observable overreach.
